paraphrase: The root expounders of the Tīrthaṅkara's word, in its collective and particular aspects, are the substance-standpoint and the mode-standpoint; the others are their subdivisions.

paraphrase: Each standpoint taken by itself, excluding the others, is false; the standpoints joined together and mutually dependent are right view — like separate gems that become a necklace only when strung together.
notes: The necklace simile recalled; exact gāthās not checked.

paraphrase: In the omniscient, knowledge and perception are not two cognitions occurring in succession or at once, but one: when all obstruction is gone, the distinction of general and particular grasping falls away.
As many as are the ways of speaking, so many are the standpoint-doctrines; as many as are the standpoint-doctrines, so many are the other doctrines (parasamaya).
notes: Number recalled (3.47).

paraphrase: Blessed be the Jina's word, which is the aggregate of the wrong views, the essence of nectar, easily reached by those who long for release.
notes: The closing gāthā of the Sanmati (numbered 69 or 70); wording recalled only in substance.

paraphrase: Valid cognition (pramāṇa) is knowledge that illuminates itself and its object and is free from contradiction; it is direct or indirect.

Twelve positions — beginning with the view that all is to be known by practice alone and running through determinism, nature, time, Īśvara, the self, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist and grammarian views — are arranged as spokes of a wheel, each overturned by the next; the Jain view is the whole wheel, in which each is valid in its place.
notes: The sequence of the twelve spokes is given from memory and is uncertain.

paraphrase: Direct cognition is of two kinds: 'conventionally direct' (sāṃvyavahārika), the knowledge through senses and mind, and 'truly direct' (mukhya), clairvoyance, mind-reading and omniscience; memory, recognition, reasoning (tarka), inference and scripture are indirect.

The Lord of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika cannot be the maker of the world: an unembodied maker cannot act, an embodied one would need a maker for his body, and the world as a whole is not shown to be an effect; nor can such a Lord be the teacher of the path, since only one freed of faults by his own effort is trustworthy.

When the brahmin Indrabhūti comes to Mahāvīra doubting that the soul exists, Mahāvīra shows that the soul is directly known through the awareness 'I', that doubt itself is a quality needing a possessor, and that the Vedic passages he misread in fact affirm it; the other ten gaṇadharas' doubts (on karma, the body, the elements, rebirth, bondage, gods, hells, merit, the other world and liberation) are resolved in turn.
notes: Summary of a long section; arguments recalled in outline only.

paraphrase: Following the scriptures, the omniscient knows and perceives in alternating moments, not simultaneously, since two cognitive activities (upayoga) cannot occur at once.
A steady state of mind is meditation (dhyāna); a moving one is thought (citta), which is either cultivation, reflection or reasoning.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Yoga is threefold: yoga by desire (icchā) of one who wishes to practise but is careless; yoga by scripture (śāstra) of the diligent who follows the texts; and yoga by capacity (sāmarthya), which goes beyond what scripture can describe and is known by one's own power.
notes: Opening verses (c. 2–12); numbers not checked.

paraphrase: Mitrā, tārā, balā, dīprā, sthirā, kāntā, prabhā and parā are the names of the views of yoga; hear their marks.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The eightfold view of the one with good view is like [the light of] a fire of straw, of cow-dung, of wood, a lamp, a gem, a star, the sun and the moon.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: For those endowed with the yogas beginning with restraint (yama), [the views] are held to be, in order, the stages of the qualities beginning with non-aversion, through the removal of the faults beginning with fatigue.
notes: The eight limbs, eight faults (kheda, udvega, kṣepa, utthāna, bhrānti, anyamud, ruj, āsaṅga) and eight qualities (adveṣa, jijñāsā, śuśrūṣā, śravaṇa, bodha, mīmāṃsā, pratipatti, pravṛtti) are listed in the commentary tradition; Haribhadra names the lists after Patañjali and the Bhadantas Bhāskara and Bandhu-Bhagavaddatta (recalled). paraphrase: In mitrā the view is dim, like a straw-fire spark; restraints are present as wish; there is no weariness in worship of the gods and the like, and no aversion to others; the 'seeds of yoga' — devotion to the Jina, service of teachers, disgust with worldly existence — are sown.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: yama; fault removed: fatigue; quality: non-aversion.

paraphrase: In tārā the view is a little clearer, like a cow-dung fire; the observances (niyama) appear, there is no anxiety in doing good, and a desire to know the truth arises.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: niyama; fault: anxiety; quality: desire to know.

paraphrase: In balā the view is firm like a wood fire; posture becomes steady, restlessness goes, and there is a longing to hear the truth.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: āsana; fault: distraction; quality: desire to hear.

paraphrase: In dīprā, like a lamp, breath-control (in the inner sense of expelling outward states and taking in inner ones) appears; there is no disturbance in meditation, and the truth is heard, yet the subtle 'knot' is not yet broken.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: prāṇāyāma; fault: agitation; quality: hearing.

paraphrase: In sthirā, like a gem, the knot is broken and right view arises; sense-withdrawal appears; to the wise all worldly doings look like children playing at houses of dust.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: pratyāhāra; fault: confusion; quality: understanding (bodha).

paraphrase: In kāntā, like a star, concentration (dhāraṇā) is firm; delight in other things ceases; the practitioner acts in the world while the mind stays fixed on dharma, and reflection (mīmāṃsā) deepens.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: dhāraṇā; fault: delight in other; quality: reflection.

paraphrase: In prabhā, like the sun, meditation (dhyāna) prevails, with its happiness; activity is free of attachment (asaṅga-anuṣṭhāna) — the state others call the peaceful flow (praśāntavāhitā), the destruction of the dissimilar (visabhāga-parikṣaya), the way of Śiva and the fixed path.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: dhyāna; fault: pain (ruj); quality: right apprehension.

paraphrase: In parā, like the moon, there is absorption (samādhi) free of attachment; the yogin passes beyond practices, attains omniscience and, renouncing even yoga (yoga-saṃnyāsa), reaches liberation.
notes: Section-level ref (verse range not checked). Correlation per YDS 16 and commentary: limb: samādhi; fault: attachment; quality: right activity.

paraphrase: The highest reality beyond worldly existence, called nirvāṇa, is by rule one only, though the words differ; it is spoken of as Sadāśiva, the supreme Brahman, the perfected self (siddhātman), suchness (tathatā) and by other names according to their meaning.
notes: Haribhadra's own statement of 'one goal, many names' — text-layer basis for the P2/P3 readings in the interpretation layer; the Jain tradition still denies that the liberated are one soul. Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The omniscient teachers [of the different schools] are not really different; their teachings vary according to the capacities of their disciples, as a physician's prescriptions vary with the patient.
notes: Numbers and the physician simile recalled; to be checked.

paraphrase: Yogins are of four kinds: those born in the family of yogins (gotra-yogin), those born with the dharma of yogins (kula-yogin), those in whom the wheel has been set in motion (pravṛttacakra) and the accomplished (niṣpanna); the teaching is for the second and third.
notes: Closing verses; numbers not checked.

paraphrase: Adhyātma, cultivation (bhāvanā), meditation, equanimity (samatā) and the ending of mental activity (vṛttisaṃkṣaya) — this yoga, because it joins [the soul] to liberation, is better in each successive stage.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Before yoga come the preliminaries (pūrvasevā): worship of teachers and gods, good conduct, austerity, and non-aversion to liberation.

paraphrase: Only a soul in its last cycle of worldly existence (caramāvarta), who no longer binds karma of the most intense kind (apunarbandhaka), is fit for yoga; for others the teaching does not take hold.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: Religious performance is of five kinds: 'poison' (done for this-worldly gain), 'venom' (for heavenly reward), mechanical non-performance, performance that is a cause [of the true], and 'nectar' (done with right understanding and longing for liberation); the first three are to be avoided.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: In the ending of mental activity the soul's activities born of the body and mind cease at their root; from it come omniscience and liberation.
In the ultimate sense (niścaya), yoga is the connection of the three — right knowledge and the others — [in the soul], because it joins [the soul] to liberation; so taught the lord of yogins.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: In the conventional sense (vyavahāra), yoga is also the causes of these — serving the teacher, hearing the scripture according to one's capacity, and the rest — since the cause is spoken of as the effect.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: All religious activity is yoga, because it joins one to liberation; but here [yoga] is especially that concerned with posture and the rest.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: In the teaching this [yoga] is fivefold: posture (sthāna), sound (ūrṇa), meaning (artha), support (ālambana) and the supportless; two of these are yoga of action, three yoga of knowledge.

paraphrase: Supportless yoga is meditation on the formless perfected soul; it leads to omniscience and then to the highest liberation, where the cessation of all yoga (ayoga) is reached.

paraphrase: The Buddhist, Naiyāyika, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Jaiminīya — these are the names of the darśanas.

paraphrase: In the Jaina darśana the deity is the Jina, free of attachment and aversion; the realities are soul, non-soul, merit, demerit, inflow, stopping, bondage, shedding and liberation; the means of knowledge are direct and indirect; and a thing is many-sided.

paraphrase: The one in whom there is no attachment giving rise to affliction, no hatred burning beings, no delusion covering right knowledge — he is called Mahādeva, whether [named] Brahmā, Viṣṇu or Śiva.

Form-based meditation contemplates the Arhat seated in the assembly hall (samavasaraṇa), radiant with his marvels; meditation on deities in passionate or fearsome forms is to be avoided, since one becomes what one meditates on.
Meditation on the formless, blissful, stainless perfected supreme self, whose nature is consciousness and joy, is formless meditation.

paraphrase: Virtuous meditation is practised as the four examinations — of the Jina's command, of the harm of passions, of the fruition of karma and of the structure of the universe — and its fruit is heavenly birth and, in time, liberation.

What was learned from the ocean of scripture and the mouth of the teacher has been shown; now the stainless reality established by experience is made known.

paraphrase: Homage to him in whom attachment and the other [passions], which make the sprout of the seed of rebirth grow, have been destroyed — whether he be Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara or the Jina.

paraphrase: The twelve reflections are the ladder to meditation: by contemplating impermanence, the lack of refuge, the round of births, aloneness and the rest the mind becomes detached and fit for meditation.
notes: Section-level ref (early sargas).

paraphrase: The meditator should be detached, of steady vows, free of the passions, knowing the realities, and should choose a solitary, undisturbed place — a mountain, cave, forest or temple — and a steady posture.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: Breath-control may steady the body and reveal omens, but those who pursue it for powers fall into distress; it agitates the mind and is not the cause of liberation, which is reached by the mind's own stillness.
notes: The text's own warnings; section-level ref (the prāṇāyāma sargas); content recalled in outline.

paraphrase: In embodied meditation the yogin performs the five concentrations — earth, fire, wind, water and the essential — burning the lotus of the eight karmas with the fire arising from the syllable 'arhaṃ' and finally seeing his own self as the pure, omniscient Siddha.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: Word-based meditation contemplates the letters and sacred mantras — the vowels on a sixteen-petalled lotus, the syllable 'arhaṃ', the praṇava, the homage to the five supreme beings — as pure objects leading the mind inward.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: Form-based meditation contemplates the omniscient Arhat in his glory; formless meditation contemplates the bodiless Siddha of pure consciousness, until meditator and meditated are not experienced as two.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: Meditation and mantra used to harm, attract, subjugate or kill others is evil meditation (asad-dhyāna); it belongs to the sorrowful and cruel meditations and binds karma.
notes: Content recalled in outline; section not located.

paraphrase: In all embodied beings the self is of three kinds: external, internal and supreme; one should attain the supreme by means of the internal, and give up the external.

paraphrase: The external self is the sense of self in the body; the internal self is the self-sense in the self, free of mental error; the supreme self is utterly pure.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: One who sleeps to worldly dealings is awake to the self; one who is awake in these dealings sleeps to the self.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The soul is other, matter is other — this is the summary of reality; whatever else is said is only its elaboration.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The soul is of three kinds; in essence every soul is the supreme self, of knowledge, and is seen when the outer self (identified with body, possessions and sectarian marks) is given up and the inner self turns to it; knowing it, one is liberated.
notes: Book-level summary.

paraphrase: Who the supreme self is, that am I; who I am, that is the supreme self.
notes: Dohā number and exact wording recalled; the identity is of each soul with its own perfected nature, not with a single world-soul.

paraphrase: The god is not in the temple, not in stone, not in plaster or painting; the Jina dwells in the temple of the body — seek him there by knowing the self, not by pilgrimage and outer rites.
notes: Paraphrase of a theme of several dohās; numbers not recalled.

paraphrase: Dharma is the nature of a thing; dharma is the tenfold [virtue] beginning with forbearance; dharma is the three jewels; dharma is the protection of living beings.

paraphrase: In the reflection on the universe the text describes the uncreated, beginningless world of six substances in the shape of a standing man, with the hells below, the middle world and the heavens above, and the abode of the liberated at the summit.
notes: Section-level summary.

paraphrase: The soul is characterised by cognition, is formless, is the doer, is the size of its body, is the enjoyer, is in worldly existence, is perfected, and naturally moves upward.
notes: Each attribute is said to hold from a particular standpoint (the commentaries). Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Since the sage attains both kinds of the means of liberation (the ultimate and the conventional) in meditation, practise meditation with an attentive mind.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Recite and meditate on the words of the supreme beings of thirty-five, sixteen, six, five, four, two and one [syllables], and others according to the teacher's instruction.
notes: Commentaries: 35 = the full five-line homage; 16 = 'arhat-siddha-ācārya-upādhyāya-sarvasādhu'; 6 = 'arihanta-siddha'; 5 = 'a-si-ā-u-sā'; 4 = 'arihanta'; 2 = 'siddha'; 1 = 'oṃ' or 'a' (recalled). Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Six travellers lost in a forest see a tree full of fruit: one thinks to uproot it, one to cut the trunk, one the branches, one the twigs, one to pluck the fruit, and one to gather what has fallen — so the six soul-colourings, from black to white, show in thought, word and deed.
notes: Numbers recalled; the Śvetāmbara form of the parable (six men and a rose-apple tree, jambū) is found in the Āvaśyaka commentarial literature (source not checked).

paraphrase: The fourteen stages of quality are: wrong view, the tasting (sāsādana), the mixed, unrestrained right view, partial restraint, careless restraint, careful restraint, the unprecedented (apūrvakaraṇa), the non-returning (anivṛtti), subtle passion, subsided delusion, destroyed delusion, the omniscient with activity and without.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The twenty-eight basic qualities of the monk are the five great vows, five carefulnesses, control of the five senses, the six essential duties, plucking the hair, nakedness, not bathing, sleeping on the ground, not cleaning the teeth, eating standing, and one meal a day.
notes: Chapter/verse recalled.

paraphrase: Death is of five kinds — the 'wise-wise' death of the omniscient, the wise death of the restrained ascetic, the wise-foolish death of the layman, the foolish death of one with right view but no vows, and the foolish-foolish death of the wrong-believer; the wise death, by one of three kinds of renunciation of food, is praised.
notes: Restricted topic: summary only; classification recalled.

paraphrase: The fast unto death is to be undertaken only when death cannot be averted, with the teacher's permission, gradually, under the care of attending ascetics (niryāpaka) who strengthen the dying one with instruction and recitation; it is ruined by fear, by longing for life or death, by desire for rewards, and by attachment.
notes: Restricted: the text's own conditions and warnings, recalled in outline; no procedure recorded.

paraphrase: For Jains all worldly custom is authoritative, provided right view is not lost and the vows are not violated.
notes: Widely quoted maxim; location in the text not checked.

paraphrase: Worship of the god, attendance on the teacher, study, restraint, austerity and giving are the six daily duties of householders.
notes: Attribution and number recalled.

paraphrase: The ultimate standpoint (niścaya) is described as the real (bhūtārtha), the conventional (vyavahāra) as the unreal (abhūtārtha).
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The disciple who, understanding both the conventional and the ultimate as they are, becomes impartial, alone obtains the full fruit of the teaching.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Because they injure the soul's own states, falsehood and the rest are all violence; they are named separately only to instruct the disciple.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The non-arising of attachment and the other [passions] is non-violence; their arising is violence — this is the essence of the Jina's teaching.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Since death is certain, one who, free of attachment and the like, acts only to thin the passions and the body does not kill himself; but one who, overcome by passion, ends his life by water, fire, poison or weapon, truly commits self-killing.
notes: Restricted: the text's own distinction. Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: As a non-Aryan cannot be made to understand except in a non-Aryan tongue, so the ultimate cannot be taught without the conventional standpoint.
notes: U35 contribution to a U34-owned text (core Adhyātma teaching). Amṛtacandra's numbering. Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

original.edition: recalled by the unit author (wording believed standard; to be checked against an edition)

paraphrase: The conventional standpoint is said to be unreal (abhūtārtha); the pure standpoint is taught as the real (bhūtārtha); the soul that takes refuge in the real is of right view.

paraphrase: Who sees the self as unbound and untouched, not other, constant, undifferentiated and unconjoined — know that as the pure standpoint.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: I am one, pure, made of perception and knowledge, ever formless; nothing else, not even an atom, is mine.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Whoever are liberated are liberated through discriminative knowledge; whoever are bound are bound through its absence.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The poet sets the Samayasāra as a drama in which the conscious self (cetana), deluded into playing the roles of non-self, recognises its own nature; he names Rājamalla's commentary as his guide.
notes: Prologue; content recalled in outline.

paraphrase: In a closing chapter added by Banārsīdās, the fourteen guṇasthānas are described so that the reader, knowing the self by niścaya, also knows where he stands on the path and does not neglect conduct.

Having received the Samayasāra with Rājamalla's commentary, Banārsīdās and his friends took only the ultimate standpoint, gave up rites, vows and restraint, and behaved without discipline — which he later judges a fall into one-sidedness.
notes: Episode as recalled; verse numbers not given.

paraphrase: When Pāṇḍe Rūpcand taught the Gommaṭasāra and the guṇasthānas, Banārsīdās says his doubt was removed and his mind became balanced, holding the pure self together with the stages of conduct.
notes: Dated 1635 in the text (recalled).

paraphrase: Among Jains themselves there are wrong views: those who hold only to the ultimate standpoint and neglect conduct (niścayābhāsī), those who hold only to outward conduct (vyavahārābhāsī), and those who mix both wrongly; the true path is knowing both in their places.
notes: Chapter number recalled.

paraphrase: Ṛṣabha, lord Jina, is my beloved; I want no other husband; once pleased he never leaves me — a love with no beginning and no end.
notes: Opening of the first stavana, recalled in substance.

paraphrase: The path of the Jina is hard to see; with human eyes it cannot be found, and argument, tradition and scriptures quarrel over it; only the divine eye of experience reveals it.
notes: Second stavana (to Ajitanātha); recalled in substance.

paraphrase: The six darśanas are called the limbs of the Jina: Sāṃkhya and Yoga his two feet, the Buddhist and the Mīmāṃsaka his two hands, the Lokāyata [the belly], and the Jaina his head; whoever unites the six limbs is the true seeker.
notes: 21st stavana (to Naminātha); the assignment of limbs is recalled and may be inexact.

paraphrase: Call him Rāma or Rahīm, Kṛṣṇa or Mahādeva, Pārśvanātha or Brahmā — it is Brahman itself; as vessels differ but the clay is one, so the names differ while the self is one in nature.
notes: Pada widely ascribed to Ānandaghana; attribution and wording uncertain. The Jain reading is that every soul shares one nature, not that there is one soul.

paraphrase: Seen by one full of being, consciousness and bliss, the world appears full; to one absorbed in borrowed splendour, it is only play.
notes: First aṣṭaka (pūrṇatā); wording recalled in substance.

paraphrase: The calf of the impartial one's mind runs after the cow of reason; the monkey-mind of the petty dogmatist drags reason by the tail.
notes: Aṣṭaka on impartiality (mādhyasthya). Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The knower takes refuge in all standpoints: attached to none, he gives each its place, and with impartial mind attains the highest bliss.
notes: Last aṣṭaka (sarvanayāśraya); recalled in substance.

paraphrase: The Jinas call adhyātma the pure activity undertaken with reference to the self by those who have thrown off the rule of delusion.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Detachment is threefold: born of suffering, born of delusion, and born of knowledge; only the last is true and lasting.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: Yoga is of two kinds, action-yoga and knowledge-yoga; action purifies and supports knowledge, and knowledge makes action fruitful; the adept rests in knowledge while action falls away of itself.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: The path is set out as four yogas — of scripture, of knowledge, of action and of equanimity — each needing the others; knowledge without action and action without knowledge are both rejected.
notes: Whole-text summary.

paraphrase: Commenting on selected sūtras of Patañjali, Yaśovijaya accepts the method of stilling the mind but corrects the doctrine: the self is a knower that changes in its modes, not an unchanging witness; the Lord is the liberated omniscient, not a creator; and liberation is the soul's own knowledge, not mere isolation.
notes: Content recalled in outline only; which sūtras are treated is not checked.

paraphrase: Against the 'Adhyātma' followers of Banārsīdās: the pure self is indeed the goal, but outer conduct, worship and the monastic order are its means; and the omniscient does take food, as scripture says.
notes: Whole-text summary, recalled in outline.

paraphrase: The three views of the omniscient's knowledge and perception — in sequence, simultaneous, and identical — are each valid from a particular standpoint and are not contrary when so understood.
notes: Recalled in outline; to be checked.

paraphrase: Knowledge of reality comes through valid cognition (pramāṇa), standpoints (naya) and placement (nikṣepa); each is set out with its divisions.
Not understanding my own nature I suffered endlessly; I bow to the holy true teacher who made that state understood.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The marks of the true teacher: knowledge of the self, equal vision, acting only as past karma unfolds, unprecedented speech, and supreme scriptural knowledge.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The one attached to opinions (matārthī) takes the outward monk or family tradition for the teacher, clings to rites or to dry talk of the self, and does not seek the true teacher.
notes: Range recalled.

paraphrase: The self-seeker (ātmārthī) seeks the true teacher, has calm of passions, longing for liberation, weariness with worldly life and compassion, and so becomes fit for self-realisation.
notes: Range recalled.

paraphrase: The soul exists, it is eternal, it is the doer of its karma, it is the enjoyer, liberation exists, and the means of liberation is the true dharma.
notes: Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: Countless salutations at the feet of the knower whose state, though in a body, is beyond the body.
notes: Closing dohā; living liberation in the body (the kevalin/sadguru). Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: When will that unprecedented occasion come, when I shall become free of all knots, outer and inner, and walk the path of the great ones with every bond cut?
notes: The poem goes on to describe the ascent to omniscience and liberation.

notes: The homage is to qualities and states, not to named persons; the Arhats precede the Siddhas because they teach the path.

notes: The cūlikā; recited by Śvetāmbaras and by many Digambaras.

paraphrase: I bow to Pārśva, remover of calamities, attended by [the yakṣa] Pārśva, freed from the dense mass of karma, destroyer of the poison of snakes, abode of auspiciousness and welfare.
notes: Wording as commonly recited (recalled).

paraphrase: Having duly bowed to the feet of the first Jina — which light up the jewels in the crowns of the bowing gods, dispel the darkness of sin, and are the support of beings sinking in the ocean of existence — I will praise him.
notes: Verses 1–2 run together; recalled in substance.

paraphrase: The sages call you the supreme person, sun-coloured, stainless, beyond darkness; by rightly attaining you alone they conquer death — there is no other auspicious path to the auspicious state.
notes: Close verbal parallel to Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8 (see borrowings). Numbering follows the common (Digambara/Śvetāmbara shared) order; recalled.

paraphrase: You are the Buddha, since the gods honour your awakened understanding; you are Śaṅkara, since you bring well-being to the three worlds; you are the Creator (Dhātṛ), since you laid down the rule of the path to bliss; clearly you alone, Lord, are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
notes: The names of other traditions' ultimates are applied to the Jina by their etymological sense — a devotional form of the many-names theme. Verse number recalled, not checked; the content is the unit author's recollection (skeleton).

paraphrase: The practitioner of these mantras must be devoted to the Jina and to his teacher, truthful, self-controlled, free of anger and deceit, courageous and discreet; the mantras given without these qualities do not bear fruit.
notes: Restricted text: only the qualifications and the text's framing are recorded, no mantras or rites. Chapter 1 (sādhaka-lakṣaṇa) recalled in outline.

paraphrase: Some foolish men say a creator made the world; but if he made it, where was he before, what material did he use, and why would a perfect being create a world of suffering? The world is uncreated, like time, without beginning or end, made of the substances.
notes: Chapter 4 of the Ādipurāṇa (verse range c. 16–40 recalled); arguments given in substance.
